item.title: Former Army boss Dan Driscoll joins OpenAI as senior counselor
item.dc:creator: Jon Harper
item.description:
In his new role, Driscoll will “work with OpenAI teams and leaders across governments, industry, academia, and allied institutions to advance practical modernization initiatives that support the buildout of democratic AI,” the company said in a press release announcing his appointment.

The post Former Army boss Dan Driscoll joins OpenAI as senior counselor appeared first on DefenseScoop.
item.content:encoded:
Dan Driscoll, who resigned from his position as secretary of the Army in August after reportedly clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, has joined ChatGPT maker OpenAI as a “senior counselor for national security modernization,” the company announced Monday.

OpenAI has been landing major deals with the Pentagon and further boosting its defense business during the second Trump administration.

For example, in June 2025 the department announced that its Chief Digital and AI Office awarded a $200 million prototype Other Transaction agreement to OpenAI Public Sector to “develop prototype frontier AI capabilities to address critical national security challenges in both warfighting and enterprise domains.”

In August of this year, officials said that users of the Pentagon’s enterprise generative artificial intelligence platform, GenAI.mil, had been given the ability to use approved versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT models on that system.

During his time as Army secretary, Driscoll launched major modernization efforts, such as the Army Transformation Initiative, the service’s drone and counter-drone marketplaces and Operation Jailbreak.

“Our Soldiers, Civilians, and their Families are our Nation’s very best, and they have inspired me every day. I am sincerely thankful for their service and sacrifice,” Driscoll wrote in a social media post shortly after his resignation as Army boss. “I had the privilege of working with them to modernize and accelerate how the Army mans, trains, and equips the most lethal fighting force on the face of the earth.”

In his new role at OpenAI, Driscoll will be “working with senior leadership and external partners to advise on how advanced AI can strengthen national and cyber security, with a particular focus on working with U.S. allies to advance its responsible use,” the company said in a press release.

In the newly created position at the firm, he’ll also “work with OpenAI teams and leaders across governments, industry, academia, and allied institutions to advance practical modernization initiatives that support the buildout of democratic AI,” and “help internal OpenAI teams understand the operational needs of global national security institutions,” per the release.

In a statement, Driscoll said that national security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past half century.

New technology will enable the military and others to “keep pace by cutting through paperwork, making sense of more information, and getting the right answer to the right person faster,” he said. “I’m joining OpenAI to help the United States and our allies put this technology to work responsibly, for the people who keep us safe.”

The post Former Army boss Dan Driscoll joins OpenAI as senior counselor appeared first on DefenseScoop.

item.title: Leonardo DRS tapped to support Army’s high-energy laser program
item.dc:creator: Jon Harper
item.description:
The company will be helping prime contractor AeroVironment under the E-HEL program.

The post Leonardo DRS tapped to support Army’s high-energy laser program appeared first on DefenseScoop.
item.content:encoded:
Leonardo DRS landed a subcontract to provide “rugged integration expertise” to support the Army’s Enduring-High Energy Laser production program, the company announced Monday.

The firm was tapped by prime contractor AeroVironment for the effort, according to a press release.

The Army announced in September that it awarded AV a nearly $500 million contract for the E-HEL program with the intent of moving the system from a prototype phase into production. Company officials at the time touted it as the first production contract for directed energy weapons in U.S. history. AV has said it expects to deliver “well into the dozens” of its LOCUST X3 laser weapon systems to the military under the deal in the coming years.

The U.S. military is pursuing new tools to counter enemy drones, which are proliferating across modern battlefields, including so-called “non-kinetic” systems like high-energy lasers. Officials envision integrating the E-HEL technology with Army platforms such as the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle or Infantry Squad Vehicle, or in palletized setups. However, there are technical challenges involved in fielding powerful lasers that can work effectively and reliably in real-world combat scenarios and meet military requirements. Under its subcontract, Leonardo DRS aims to help address those issues.

“Evolving drone threats demand systems that deliver reliable performance in demanding operational environments,” Aaron Hankins, vice president and general manager for the company’s land systems business, said in a statement. “Our team is applying experience in vehicle integration, power and thermal management to help AV deliver a mobile high-energy laser capability for the U.S. Army.”

Leonardo DRS and AV did not immediately respond to questions Monday about the dollar value of the subcontract.

In a press release, Leonardo DRS noted that it has previous experience working on DE efforts, including a rapid prototyping initiative in recent years to integrate a high-energy laser into an armored vehicle for live-fire evaluations.

Separately, the Pentagon announced last month that AV’s Palletized High-Energy Laser system was one of the platforms chosen for a pilot led by Joint Interagency Task Force 401. The other DE technologies selected for the effort include the Epirus Leonidas High-Powered Microwave system, the Kord Firefly High-Energy Laser system, and the Boeing Compact Laser Weapon system, according to a Defense Department press release.

“High-energy lasers and high-powered microwave systems are tools that can be effectively used in a layered drone defense,” Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF 401, said in a statement that accompanied last month’s announcement. “This pilot program will test these capabilities in an operational environment so we can understand how best to integrate and sustain them to defend the homeland.”

As part of its efforts to assess these types of counter-drone capabilities, the task force plans to hold a directed energy “shoot-off” later this year.

The post Leonardo DRS tapped to support Army’s high-energy laser program appeared first on DefenseScoop.

item.title: How can we trust AI in national defense missions?
item.dc:creator: Billy Mitchell
item.description:
You can’t evaluate what you can’t inspect. You can’t defend a decision you can’t explain. You can’t correct a failure you can’t see. And an answer you can’t trace is an answer you can’t trust.

The post How can we trust AI in national defense missions? appeared first on DefenseScoop.
item.content:encoded:
According to recent media reports, false intelligence generated by AI came close to causing a military confrontation with China this spring. Thinking a Chinese ship in the Middle East was carrying components for nuclear weapons, the U.S. military was prepared to board the vessel. Just before the operation was launched, it was discovered that a chatbot had inaccurately identified the ship’s cargo.

With the Department of War (DoW) aggressively pushing to implement AI across all levels, we cannot assume that close calls like this one will be isolated incidents. What’s needed is a transparent and verified way to answer the question: How can we trust AI in national defense missions?

Two Levels of Decision-Making

To answer that question, some have suggested two factors for consideration: the reversibility of the decision and its consequences. Reversible and non-consequential decisions can reside with AI, while non-reversible and highly consequential decisions should reside with the “human in the loop.”

This looks and sounds reasonable, but it oversimplifies a highly complex problem. For example, if we trust AI to make all the decisions for easily reversed simple challenges, that’s ok on the micro level – but the scale of risk increases exponentially if all these lesser decisions are factored into an irrevocable high-impact decision. These lesser decisions might be low-consequence and easily reversed, but it’s a fallacy to assume the logic required to make every low-impact decision is equally simple and clear.

Adding to this complexity, security questions are rarely a single input-output operation, especially in military decision-making processes involving sensor data, intelligence, and reporting, at a minimum. When AI is involved here, the process is understood in key stages:

  • Information Collection
  • Mission analysis
  • Course of Action (COA) Development
  • COA Analysis and Comparison
  • Decision and Orders Production
  • Execution and Assessment

This is a dynamic process, with interconnected decisions that need to be executed at mission speed, with the expectation that all the factors leading to the final decision will need to withstand scrutiny at a future date.

Amidst this backdrop, it’s easy to see how unchecked AI decision-making – even with low consequence and reversible decisions – compounds risk throughout the process, ultimately leading to bad outcomes. The decision chain for any high-stakes decision is only as strong as its weakest link. One bad decision in a chain can condition future outputs, ultimately leading the “human in the loop” to a final decision with consequences that might result in the loss of innocent life, investigations and committee hearings.

You can’t evaluate what you can’t inspect. You can’t defend a decision you can’t explain. You can’t correct a failure you can’t see. And an answer you can’t trace is an answer you can’t trust.

Inaccurate and Unexplainable

According to the Stanford University Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, “AI models struggle to tell the difference between knowledge and belief,” and its new accuracy benchmark indicates that “hallucination rates across 26 top models range from 22% to 94%.”

The “State of AI in 2025 – Agents, Innovation and Transformation” report from McKinsey Consulting uncovers two glaring problems with the implementation of AI – inaccuracy and a lack of understanding where the answers are coming from: “Inaccuracy is one of two risks that most respondents say their organizations are working to mitigate. However, the second-most-commonly-reported risk— explainability—is not among the most commonly mitigated.”

The entire point of using AI to support intelligence missions is to support overburdened human decision-makers so they can make better decisions faster. So, we must identify when the smaller “reversible and non-consequential” decisions can be trusted, and when further investigation is required, so that intelligence analysts can advance with confidence. Otherwise, we run a high risk of increasing cognitive load and overburdening analysts at a time when lives are at risk.

Capabilities that Provide Trust

What is needed then is a method to make AI trusted. For AI to be trusted, you have to be able to account for four factors behind every answer:

  1. The data it learned from
  2. The context it was given
  3. The model that produced it
  4. The actions an agent took on it

Most AI systems, frontier models included, cover one or two of these at best. What they offer is data traceability, which amounts to ‘I think the answer came from this source,’ and models often hallucinate about that too. That doesn’t go far enough to explain an answer. Provenance and lineage have to run through all four factors as described. When they do, you get explainability. And when that explainability stays with your data, under the laws of the nation that governs it, you get sovereignty.

Most organizations get the trust question backwards – in short, they are asking users to trust AI, without giving them the evidence to verify it. Too often, AI is deployed and operated on assumed trust: the vendor says it works, the answer sounds confident, and everyone moves on. AI shouldn’t be making high-stakes decisions without passing high levels of scrutiny and accountability. “The model said so” won’t hold up in a military investigation.

No one – especially not military decision-makers – should use a system they can’t trust. Evaluation tools and systems need to arm and assist the human in the loop. A well-tested, explainable and transparent system codifies our laws and ethics, providing the guardrails and guidelines required to provide operational deployment with minimal risk.

The post How can we trust AI in national defense missions? appeared first on DefenseScoop.

item.title: The missing puzzle piece in space superiority: Why it’s time for the U.S. government to prioritize VLEO
item.dc:creator: Jon Harper
item.description:
A nuclear detonation in space could make all of LEO unusable for up to a year.

The post The missing puzzle piece in space superiority: Why it’s time for the U.S. government to prioritize VLEO appeared first on DefenseScoop.
item.content:encoded:
Over the past decade, the United States has come to recognize that space is no longer a sanctuary. China and Russia are developing weapons to disrupt, disable and destroy American satellites. The Space Force now talks openly about weapons in space, orbital warfare, and space superiority. Just last month, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink stated for the first time that the Space Force “has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.”

Government funding has followed. The Space Force’s fiscal 2027 budget request, at $71.1 billion, is a 124% increase from fiscal 2026 and the largest percentage increase for a service since 1952. Hundreds of new satellites are being deployed to make American space architecture more distributed and resilient, while the Space Force explores new concepts focused on making space operations more agile, proliferated, and intelligent. With space more accessible and affordable, the Space Force and commercial companies alike are proliferating the vast majority of new satellites to Low Earth Orbit (LEO), which demands large numbers of spacecraft for persistent coverage over a given region.

But this space superiority strategy does not account for the most significant threat in space: a nuclear detonation that makes all of LEO unusable for up to a year.

This is not a hypothetical risk. In 2022, Russia deployed a test-bed satellite to learn how it could deploy a nuclear weapon in space. Two years later, the Pentagon confirmed that Russia was developing an “indiscriminate” nuclear weapon to deploy in LEO. And in March of this year, Gen. Stephen Whiting, commander of U.S. Space Command, called the prospect of a nuclear weapon on orbit the “single greatest threat to our space architecture.”

For all the attention Washington rightly devotes to jamming, cyberattacks, rendezvous and proximity operations, conventional anti-satellite weapons, and a responsive space industrial base — none could counter this single greatest threat.

A nuclear detonation in LEO, where most satellites today reside, would do more than destroy satellites in the immediate line of sight. It would inject high-energy electrons into Earth’s magnetic field, creating artificial radiation belts that persist for up to a year. Most commercial-style LEO satellites, designed for the natural radiation environment, would begin failing in days or weeks. The space industry would largely ground to a halt.

The United States is investing heavily in the ability to manufacture and launch replacement satellites quickly — an effort known as “Tactically Responsive Space” (TacRS). But after a high-altitude nuclear event, newly launched conventional LEO spacecraft would encounter the same radiation environment that destroyed their predecessors. The underlying radiation can persist on roughly year-long timescales: one recent Atlantic Council analysis cites particle diffusion approaching 300 days in LEO. Building more satellites faster will not provide resilience when those satellites do not have a survivable orbit to deploy to.

The good news is that the U.S. has an alternative: building infrastructure in a lower, more resilient orbit.

Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) generally refers to the region below roughly 350 kilometers, and the most interesting survivability benefits appear around 300 kilometers and below. At these altitudes, the Earth’s atmosphere is dense enough to absorb the harmful radiation, a natural shield for satellites flying in VLEO.

A nuclear detonation could still destroy some satellites within line-of-sight of the immediate detonation, but VLEO would largely remain reusable after an attack. Surviving satellites could continue operating, and replacements can be launched without waiting months for an artificial radiation environment to subside.

Despite the fact that VLEO could de-risk the most significant threat to space operations, the Space Force and Intelligence Community have not historically paid nearly as much attention to it. The U.S. government has invested a few million dollars into R&D projects but very little relative to larger space expenditures. In his first major remarks as chief of space operations, Gen. Douglas Schiess described the Space Force’s mandate as protecting space “from low Earth orbit all the way out to cislunar space,” leaving out VLEO.

China recognizes the advantages of VLEO. Its state-owned aerospace industry is pursuing a planned 300-satellite VLEO remote-sensing constellation by 2030, and in June China formed a 34-member VLEO technology and industrial alliance to coordinate research, standards and commercialization. Public reporting on China’s Chutian constellation describes plans for optical, radar, hyperspectral and infrared sensing from below 300 kilometers. This commitment to VLEO dwarfs that of the U.S. While China’s future proliferation of VLEO is not the only reason to act, it compounds the risk of the U.S. losing LEO in a conflict, as China would have an asymmetric, survivable orbital layer.

The Space Force and Intelligence Community should treat orbital diversity the same way military planners treat geographic diversity. We would never place every critical aircraft at one air base simply because that base was highly defended. Yet an enormous share of U.S. communications, sensing, missile warning, targeting capability, and exquisite satellites is concentrating in broadly similar LEO environments.

A VLEO layer could replicate a subset of the most essential missions — targeting and damage assessment, intelligence and surveillance, tactical communications, missile tracking and space-domain awareness — so that losing access to conventional LEO would not mean losing those capabilities altogether. Beyond redundancy, flying below other satellites offers a useful vantage point for sensors looking upward into LEO. And proximity to Earth brings secondary advantages including stronger signals, higher imaging resolution and lower communications latency. While higher orbits like Medium Earth Orbit (MEO) and Geostationary Orbit (GEO) also offer redundancy, they lack the same cost advantages of deploying to LEO or VLEO, as well as the advantages in resolution and latency that are inherent with proximity to Earth.

VLEO technology is much less speculative than it was a decade ago. This orbit imposes punishing atmospheric drag and atomic-oxygen exposure, which has historically made long-duration operations difficult. Commercial flight demonstrations, including just last year from Albedo (a Shield Capital portfolio company), have now validated key technologies for sustained operations in the regime at a price point that is competitive with LEO offerings and much less expensive than MEO or GEO. Meanwhile, DARPA is developing new propulsion approaches that will make VLEO even more tractable.

To their credit, Space Force officials are beginning to recognize the opportunity. Deputy Chief Science Officer Gillian Bussey recently described VLEO as a way to create a “resilient and survivable architecture” and suggested rapidly deploying proliferated VLEO systems after losing imaging or communications satellites elsewhere. The service plans to further develop its VLEO architecture plans in the next year.

Additionally, the White House has now set the direction for VLEO. A December executive order explicitly directed the government to ensure the ability to address threats from VLEO through cislunar space, including nuclear weapons, while creating a more responsive and adaptive national-security space architecture. Statements like these are early signals that the U.S. government wants to make VLEO a core part of its strategy for space superiority.

If the U.S. fails to prioritize VLEO imminently, it would not be the first time Chinese industrial policy spent years building advantages in technologies Washington regarded as interesting but strategically secondary. By the time inexpensive Chinese drones became indispensable on battlefields around the world, DJI already dominated the market. To this day, U.S. and Ukrainian drone supply chains are critically dependent on China, which is also directly and indirectly supporting the Russian military.

We are at risk of making a mistake in VLEO that could have similar consequences.

The Space Force does not need to move everything into VLEO. It needs to ensure that the U.S. can maintain critical operations from space even if it loses access to LEO. That means identifying the missions that must survive even if conventional LEO becomes temporarily inaccessible, funding VLEO spacecraft and constellations, establishing operational experience, and building a domestic industrial base for production capacity.

The U.S. cannot achieve space superiority if it ignores the largest threat to an indispensable orbit. Space superiority means retaining essential capability after an adversary tries to destroy it. VLEO is a challenging but proven orbit, and the Space Force’s investments should reflect its importance.

David Rothzeid is a Principal at Shield Capital, an early-stage venture fund focused on the intersection of national security and commercial capability. He served in the United States Air Force as an acquisition officer for over a dozen years and is currently a reservist at the Pentagon.

Matt Kaplan is an Associate at Shield Capital.

The post The missing puzzle piece in space superiority: Why it’s time for the U.S. government to prioritize VLEO appeared first on DefenseScoop.

item.title: Army selects Lockheed Martin for billion-dollar Future Interceptor program
item.dc:creator: Jon Harper
item.description:
Under a cost-sharing arrangement, Lockheed is expected to kick in $423 million for the project while Uncle Sam provides about $660 million.

The post Army selects Lockheed Martin for billion-dollar Future Interceptor program appeared first on DefenseScoop.
item.content:encoded:
The Army gave the nod to Lockheed Martin to further develop a new missile interceptor that’s expected to have better engagement range, altitude, velocity and maneuverability than legacy systems, the service announced Thursday.

The contractor secured an Other Transaction agreement for the Future Interceptor program.

The total project value is estimated to exceed $1 billion. Under a cost-sharing arrangement, Lockheed is expected to kick in $423 million while Uncle Sam provides about $660 million, according to an Army press release.

The initiative comes as America’s adversaries are developing more capable missiles and unmanned aerial systems, including hypersonics, next-generation ballistic missiles and cruise missiles, and jet-powered attack drones. The Army, which provides much of the U.S. military’s ground-based air-and-missile defense systems, is pursuing new weapons that can defeat those types of threats.

“Developing advanced interceptor capabilities is essential to maintaining our nation’s defensive advantage against increasingly sophisticated threats,” Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, portfolio acquisition executive for fires, said in a statement. “The Future Interceptor program reflects the Army’s commitment to accelerating innovation, leveraging proven technologies and strengthening the layered defenses that protect our forces and national interests at home and abroad.”

Brent Ingraham, the Army’s acquisition chief, said in a statement that the contract award announced Thursday was an important step in the service’s push to deliver new systems for integrated air-and-missile defense.

“Under the agreement, the Army will work with Lockheed Martin to advance prototype development and conduct testing and evaluation to assess system performance against established operational requirements,” officials wrote in an Army press release.

“Future development and production decisions will be informed by prototype performance, operational requirements, available resources and applicable acquisition processes,” per the release.

Lockheed Martin previously announced that it was offering its new PAC-3 Edge system for the Future Interceptor program, saying in a press release issued earlier this month that the company planned to begin testing the weapon in 2027 with the aim of having it ready for deployment by 2031.

The contractor’s Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) family of systems has been a cornerstone of the Army’s and international partners’ air-and-missile defense architectures for many years. Most recently, they’ve played a significant role in conflicts with Iran in the Middle East and the war in Ukraine.

According to a Lockheed Martin press release issued Oct. 9, the PAC-3 Edge is a next-generation system that will provide greater maneuverability, power, velocity and precision, and come with an advanced seeker, multi-pulse solid rocket motor, and control system upgrades.

“PAC-3 Edge is designed to be integrated with existing and future IAMD capabilities including the Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), the M903 launcher, containerized launchers and HIMARS Flex,” per the Lockheed press release.

The post Army selects Lockheed Martin for billion-dollar Future Interceptor program appeared first on DefenseScoop.

item.title: GDIT puts Vion mission partner environment technology through its paces during Pacific exercise
item.dc:creator: Jon Harper
item.description:
The tech stack includes deployable cloud hardware, a secure zero-trust platform, common data-centric services, and C2 mission applications, a company official told DefenseScoop.

The post GDIT puts Vion mission partner environment technology through its paces during Pacific exercise appeared first on DefenseScoop.
item.content:encoded:
General Dynamics Information Technology’s Vion mission partner environment kit was incorporated into the U.S. military’s recent Olympus Fires exercise in the Pacific, the company announced Thursday.

The exercise came as the Defense Information Systems Agency and other military components are working to boost information sharing among allies.

The demonstration of GDIT’s Vion system capabilities was the culmination of years of effort and internal investment by the company, according to Jason Myers, vice president of GDIT’s defense agencies business.

“We’re actually selling it as that integrated hardware and software bundle. So, kind of view it as four different layers, if you will, of the … mission-ready tech stack: deployable cloud hardware, a secure zero-trust platform, the common data-centric services, and then the [command-and-control] mission applications,” Myers said in an interview ahead of the official announcement.

“A lot of these pieces have really been in the works. But one of the things that was really critical to me this year was really doubling down to make sure that we’re putting this into users’ hands. And so that’s where a lot of these culminations really came together. And then we had certain goals we wanted to set for ourselves. You know … it’s easy to say ‘zero trust,’ it’s easy to say ‘AI.’ You know, they’re very buzzwordy. But how do you actually operationalize them? How do you influence a mission advantage? And that’s where we really felt like we came together … and we wanted to test that out at exercise and prove it. And now we feel very comfortable with what we’ve been able to go ahead and demonstrate,” he added.

The deployment of the Vion system in an exercise had multiple elements to it.

“First and foremost is the ability to have our own core services, right? So, when we talk about our own core services, it’s having secure AI-enabled collaboration tools, so offering real-time translation services. One of the things that people take for granted on translation is it’s been around a very long time. But that being said, it’s very tabular in nature, right? X word equals Y other word. And in the military context, that’s really difficult. Military jargon, acronyms, codes — all of those things really do play and complicate typical translation services. And so, having AI assistance to understand the context of what you’re trying to say was really, really paramount. And we used that with a number of our foreign partners,” Myers told DefenseScoop.

The tech offers advanced voice, video, chat and email collaboration tools, according to GDIT.

AI-assisted software development is another capability Vion brings to the table, Myers noted.

Recent real-world conflicts have highlighted the importance of software innovation.

“There are certain elements where, as we’ve seen in Ukraine, the ability to adapt, overcome [is critical]. You’re going to have new sensors, you’re going to have new drone feeds, you’re going to have all these things that you’re going to have to provide the warfighter, but you’re not going to have … a software development team necessarily sitting there next to those warfighters. So, how do you give somebody that’s maybe never developed before, the ability to go and build that? And that’s exactly what we were able to demonstrate on Vion with the exercise. And probably the most paramount one was how do you solve problems rapidly?” Myers said.

“There were a number of customers that had interesting dynamics with their network. And they were able to take all of their network diagnostics, put it into Vion and our … secure AI-assisted platform, and not just identify what the problem was, but actually get [information telling them] here’s what you need to go fix, here’s what the fix is,” he said.

As an example, Myers described a situation where some video elements were impacted.

“We were able to use AI to say, ‘here’s the problem, here’s some of the logs,’ and within minutes we were back up and running and able to federate those services again,” he told DefenseScoop.

Zero trust and identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) are key elements of the tools, Myers suggested.

“Anybody that has a laptop and is connected to Vion has access to all of our foundational capabilities. But really the major advancement as well is the ability to then federate those services with our foreign partners. So now our foreign partners actually can reach into Vion and get access to those services as well,” he said.

An aim is to prevent under-sharing and over-sharing of sensitive information.

“By using our identity management, we know exactly who is trying to request access, and then leveraging that with the data tagging on the back end, we’re able to make sure that only those right partners with the right clearances and the right accesses can get access to that data,” Myers told DefenseScoop.

GDIT sees a lot of demand from the U.S. military and its allies for the types of capabilities that Vion offers, Myers said, though he declined to identify specific potential customers the company is in talks with.

The firm used its own money to develop Vion, he noted, an indication that the contractor had confidence that it could sell it to government buyers.

“I wanted to take a risk, right? I wanted to go and say ‘we know the customer space, we know what you need,’” Myers explained. “Vion was completely built by GDIT, and we had to go prove [the effectiveness of the technology] in exercise.”

GDIT isn’t fully on contract with the Pentagon for the Vion system, he told DefenseScoop.

“Now the next steps are, we’ve got a couple customers who have actually stated that they plan on supporting our accreditation and broader scale deployment across a number of different organizations,” Myers said. “Our focus was let’s prove it. And now the customer has said ‘you did prove it [and] we’re going to help you scale this.’”

The post GDIT puts Vion mission partner environment technology through its paces during Pacific exercise appeared first on DefenseScoop.

item.title: Army designates 2 additional ‘permissive’ sites for commercial vendors to test their drone and counter-drone tech
item.dc:creator: Jon Harper
item.description:
The move is part of a broader Army initiative aimed at facilitating vendor access to test ranges.

The post Army designates 2 additional ‘permissive’ sites for commercial vendors to test their drone and counter-drone tech appeared first on DefenseScoop.
item.content:encoded:
The Army designated Camp Atterbury Joint Maneuver Training Center and Muscatatuck Training Center as “premier, permissive sites available for commercial testing” of drone and counter-drone systems, the service announced Wednesday.

The move is part of a broader Army initiative to facilitate vendor access to test ranges as the service races to add new unmanned aerial systems and counter-UAS tools to its arsenal.

The Camp Atterbury Joint Maneuver Training Center and Muscatatuck Training Center are both located in Indiana.

Other locations with test ranges that fall under the initiative include Camp Grayling in Michigan, Dugway Proving Ground in Utah, Arizona’s West Cibola Range, Camp Shelby in Mississippi, and the Africa Multidomain Training and Experimentation Center (AMTEC) in Morocco.

Prior to his resignation as Army secretary, Dan Driscoll pushed to make it easier for vendors to get access to Army locations where they can put their technologies through their paces.

“Sometimes it can take 12 to 18 months for a company that wants to go test the thing that can make a soldier’s life better, that can increase their lethality, and that can keep them safer,” Driscoll said in August. “That is not sufficient.”

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle, who was appointed to his position after Driscoll’s departure, announced the additions to the Army’s Permissive Test Range Expansion Initiative on Wednesday.

“The sites selected for inclusion provide specialized capabilities to facilitate drone and counter-drone testing. Camp Atterbury offers more than 34,000 acres of secure space with a dedicated restricted airspace corridor up to 40,000 feet. The Muscatatuck Training Center is a 1,000-acre developmental testing site featuring configurable urban infrastructure, which allows testing of drone and counter-drone navigation and tracking systems within complex physical and structural layouts,” officials wrote in a press release.

Vendors can request access to the sites at Atterbury, Muscatatuck, or other locations that are part of the initiative via an online portal: testrange.army.mil. Army Test and Evaluation Command (ATEC) has created a so-called “concierge team” to assist companies with the scheduling process.

“Once a request is submitted, the dedicated ATEC private industry concierge team will work with the vendor and Indiana National Guard to coordinate testing schedules and requirements,” officials wrote in the press release.

“While submitting a request does not guarantee a vendor’s desired location or timeline due to capacity limits, the concierge team will work closely with all applicants to find suitable testing locations and windows,” per the release.

The post Army designates 2 additional ‘permissive’ sites for commercial vendors to test their drone and counter-drone tech appeared first on DefenseScoop.

item.title: U.S. military building resilience against emerging OPSEC risks from automated surveillance networks
item.dc:creator: Jon Harper
item.description:
Frontier AI and other advanced technologies are making it easier for adversaries to find and exploit vulnerabilities associated with those interconnected capabilities.

The post U.S. military building resilience against emerging OPSEC risks from automated surveillance networks appeared first on DefenseScoop.
item.content:encoded:
GRAPEVINE, Texas — The U.S. government and law enforcement agencies are increasingly utilizing commercial surveillance products that fuse computer vision, pattern tracking and behavioral analysis assets to support public safety and other operations. 

That ever-growing network of integrated cameras, sensors and other tech is simultaneously introducing new security risks across the joint force.

“Everything has a vulnerability,” a U.S. Transportation Command official told DefenseScoop on Tuesday. “You just have to understand what it is, and exploit it.”

On the sidelines of the annual Fall Meeting co-hosted by the National Defense Transportation Association and Transcom this week, multiple officials from that combatant command discussed countering threats against military personnel and logistics posed by AI-enabled capabilities that trace patterns of movement en masse. They requested anonymity to speak freely about their concerns.

Their comments come as automated license plate readers, cloud-connected surveillance hardware and AI-enabled tracking tools (from companies like Flock Safety, Axon and Motorola Solutions) are being widely integrated across America and used by police departments, neighborhood homeowners associations, business districts, and private entities.

“It’s analogous to a picket line, which would be a series of observers along specific routes that can report back,” a Transcom official said. “These cameras kind of do the same thing — they run software [for] optical character recognition, so they can read your [license] plate data.”

While these technologies are designed and marketed for crime detection and civilian neighborhood protection, their dense networks of interconnected devices present new operational security risks for the U.S. military’s personnel and assets. 

Transcom’s mission hinges on coordinating strategic air, land, and sea transportation for troops and weapons worldwide, during peacetime and war.

According to the officials who spoke to DefenseScoop this week, the commercial surveillance technologies are enabling easier pattern-of-life tracking of service members — as well as force movement and unit deployment indicators that can reveal sensitive information to adversaries paying attention about training schedules and mobilization plans.

“For me, it’s understanding the mission threats, understanding that infrastructure,” a Transcom official said. “I mean, companies are going to secure their networks and things of that nature, but what does that data traverse across? Those are your choke points that you can exploit.”

Another Transcom source noted that frontier models and other advanced AI capabilities are also helping bad actors capitalize on certain data vulnerabilities at a larger scale than what’s been done before. 

“I’m really not as concerned about, ‘can you see my tag?’ It’s about if you are able to understand what that tag is tied to from an intent and timing” perspective, the Transcom official said. “Other than that, it’s a great opportunity because there are a lot of bees in that swarm.”

When asked how the command is thinking creatively about resilience and countering these modern threats as the network continues to expand, officials pointed to initiatives to protect sensitive context around military movement data and diversify geographic locations, ports, and airfields to get ahead of potential effects of localized disruptions — including cyber incidents or power failures.

They also cited a need for more whole-of-government engagement opportunities with local and private infrastructure partners. 

“There are some real policy [aspects] that we need to start to look at that will enable our actions and make it harder for somebody trying to exploit or operationalize that opportunity. The other portion of it is, at Transcom, you have to get very comfortable with the amount of data that you usually would never allow somebody to have their hands on — because it’s just the way logistics is,” an official told DefenseScoop.

Spokespersons from Flock, Axon and Motorola did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Wednesday.

The post U.S. military building resilience against emerging OPSEC risks from automated surveillance networks appeared first on DefenseScoop.

item.title: Army taps AWS and WWT to boost AI-enabled cybersecurity initiative
item.dc:creator: Jon Harper
item.description:
“Partnering with commercial industry is a national security imperative for the Army, as the private sector drives rapid innovation in superintelligence, cloud architecture and cyber operations capabilities,” Col. David Bergmann said.

The post Army taps AWS and WWT to boost AI-enabled cybersecurity initiative appeared first on DefenseScoop.
item.content:encoded:
The Army’s Project Griffin is moving forward with the selection of Amazon Web Services and World Wide Technology to support the AI-enabled cybersecurity initiative, the service announced this week.

The pilot effort, which has a combined total value of $2.6 million, falls under the Army Rapid Development of Cyber Defense Systems (ARDS) program and is driven by the project manager for cyber warfare under the portfolio management executive for intelligence and spectrum warfare.

“Project Griffin is one of the first efforts under Project ARDS, which is advancing the Army’s adoption of SI-enabled cyber defense capabilities through rapid sprints in conjunction with industry partners,” Brandon Pugh, the secretary of the Army’s principal cyber advisor, said in a statement, using an acronym to refer to super intelligence, which is the Trump administration’s preferred name for artificial intelligence.

“We will swiftly implement SI-enabled cyber tools to detect, divert and deceive threat actors, and rapidly adopt agentic SI to securely scale network defense and disruption. The selection of AWS and WWT allows us to move at the speed of business required to deliver that capability,” Pugh added.

Army Cyber Command is also involved in the initiative.

Project Griffin is moving forward as defense officials try to confront the growing threat of potential AI-enabled digital attacks in cyberspace against their systems.

The Army aims to develop an ecosystem of agents that will use information gleaned from its panoply of network sensors and take defensive measures to thwart potential threats, faster than a human operator can.

The department released a solicitation in August seeking agentic AI solutions for an Intelligent Response and Orchestration Node (IRON) capability under Project Griffin.

At the annual AUSA conference in Washington earlier this month, Pugh said the Army received over 100 industry submissions, ultimately picking two vendors. He did not identify the awardees at the time.

Defense officials are keen to tap into the expertise of the commercial sector.

“Partnering with commercial industry is a national security imperative for the Army, as the private sector drives rapid innovation in superintelligence, cloud architecture and cyber operations capabilities,” Col. David Bergmann, project manager for cyber warfare, said in a statement accompanying this week’s announcement about the selection of AWS and WWT.

“Through our flexible procurement methods, we were able to quickly seek out SI solutions that will advance the cyber warfighter. Working with industry guarantees the Army maintains technological overmatch and secures the modern digital high ground against adversaries,” he added.

Media and PR officials at AWS and WWT did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday.

Keith Linenberger, an area vice president at WWT, highlighted the company’s selection for Project Griffin in a post on LinkedIn.

“WWT is partnering with Crogl to deliver API- and MCP-based integrations connecting AI agents with the tools and data cyber teams rely on. This prototype is an exciting opportunity to help translate emerging AI capabilities into operational impact and mirrors similar efforts we are delivering in the [U.S. Air Force],” he wrote. 

The post Army taps AWS and WWT to boost AI-enabled cybersecurity initiative appeared first on DefenseScoop.

item.title: Air Force launches next phase of hypersonic missile program with $694M contract award for ARRW
item.dc:creator: Jon Harper
item.description:
DefenseScoop talked to analysts about the implications of the deal.

The post Air Force launches next phase of hypersonic missile program with $694M contract award for ARRW appeared first on DefenseScoop.
item.content:encoded:
The Air Force recently took a major step in its pursuit of hypersonic missiles, awarding Lockheed Martin a $694 million production contract for a boost-glide system that can be carried by B-52 bombers.

The deal for the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon (ARRW) was awarded Sept. 29, according to a press release, although the service didn’t announce it until Monday.

The announcement withheld key details about the contract, such as quantities of missile purchases and delivery dates, citing a need to protect “operational security.”

The award is the latest turn in the saga of the ARRW program, which at one time seemed like it might not survive the budgetary axe following a series of setbacks during its development phase — including at least one failed all-up-round flight test that occurred in 2023 — and the prioritization of another initiative known as the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM).

However, the program was revived, and officials requested funding from Congress in fiscal 2026 to start production. The award for the new production contract came in the final days of fiscal 2026.

“This is a turning point in our advanced weapons roadmap,” Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said in a statement released Monday. “By moving ARRW from test to production, we’re providing our combatant commanders with a credible, high-speed strike weapon capable of penetrating the most advanced anti-access and area-denial systems.”

The Pentagon has invested billions of dollars to develop hypersonic weapons. In addition to the air-launched ARRW and HACM, other hypersonic systems that the military is working to field include the Army’s ground-launched Dark Eagle and the Navy’s sea-launched Conventional Prompt Strike.

Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach said in a statement Monday that fielding ARRW will enhance the service’s ability to “hold targets at risk anywhere around the world” and provide the joint force with a “flexible and rapid response option for highly contested environments.”

In a press release issued Tuesday, Lockheed Martin said the system brings “sustained and maneuverable hypersonic capabilities to America’s Arsenal of Freedom and is the culmination of years of developmental and test partnership between Lockheed Martin and the U.S. Air Force.”

Mark Gunzinger, director for future concepts and capability assessments at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies and a former deputy assistant secretary of defense, called the production contract award “a real turning point” for the Air Force and the Pentagon.

The U.S. military needs an operational air-launched hypersonic weapon to create a future strike force capable of high-intensity warfare against peer adversaries like China, Russia, and others, he told DefenseScoop.

“Frankly, hypersonic weapons is one such capability where China has stolen a march on the United States, and I think this announcement is a real milestone in that effort to catch up and maintain our advantage, technological advantage as well as operational advantages over China. That’s exactly what we need to do to deter possible conflict in the Pacific,” Gunzinger added.

Hypersonics are intended to be highly survivable, he noted, “which is a combination of their speed and actual designs to reduce their signatures and so forth.”

They would most likely be used against “fleeting” or “time-sensitive” targets, Gunzinger said, such as highly mobile and relocatable weapon systems like missile launchers, and command-and-control platforms.

Carlton Haelig, a fellow in the Defense Program at the Center for a New American Security, said the movement of ARRW into production is “hugely” significant.

“In general, it’s a big step forward because it provides a, you know, more diverse capability set, but particularly just in the Air Force trying to get itself established and having operational hypersonic weapons capability,” Haelig told DefenseScoop.

Just a few years ago, the ARRW program appeared to be shelved, he noted.

“They were indicating that they were not going to be moving it to operational use. They concluded its [research, development, test and evaluation] spending. There were some failed or unsuccessful tests, and they were kind of cutting their losses and moving on to other programs. Now, sometime between then and last year when the budget documentation came out … obviously things changed,” he said. “Obviously through their testing and evaluation, they’ve identified that they have a viable, safe and effective platform that they’re comfortable with moving into initial procurement.”

Haelig noted that sometimes the military services keep programs in the research and development stage longer than they need to be, and that increases the costs associated with those programs and delays their eventual transition into the field and throughout the force.

“So, this could also be the type of decision where they say, ‘Look, we have enough ready to go forward with the Block A variant of ARRW. It’s ready, it’s safe, it’s effective. It can be integrated onto the platforms. Let’s move forward with this, and we’ll continue to iterate on what might eventually be a Block B. We don’t need that Block B solution to get in the way of the Block A capability’ that they seem to have available to them right now,” Haelig told DefenseScoop.

Gunzinger noted that ARRW systems will come with a relatively high price tag compared to many other types of munitions. His “informed guess” is that they’ll cost “well over $10 million a copy.”

They’re not an “affordable mass munition,” in Air Force parlance, he said.

“They’re not going to be a level-of-effort munition that you size their inventory for a large-scale air campaign. They are special capabilities to be used against the … highest value, critical targets that we absolutely need to destroy in order to take down an adversary’s A2AD network and disrupt their command and control, battlespace management operations, and so forth,” he said.

The B-52 Stratofortress, which has already been used for ARRW testing, is well-suited to carry the missile, according to Gunzinger.

“It’s obvious that the B-52 would be the initial aircraft for integrating this weapon into the Air Force’s arsenal. They’ll be the threshold aircraft because they are very large weapons, and they have to be carried externally because of that, and you would not want to obviously carry ARRW externally on … a B-21 [Raider] or, you know, another aircraft that is stealthy, because that would essentially really create a signature that’s no longer stealthy,” he said.

The Stratofortress could potentially carry multiple ARRWs, according to Gunzinger, who said the B-1 Lancer could also carry the missile.

Based on the size of the contract, he estimated that the Air Force is probably buying “dozens” of ARRW missiles with this new production deal but less than 100, depending on their exact cost.

Haelig said the number of ARRWs being purchased with the new contract is “certainly not hundreds” but “definitely double digits.”

He noted that some of the funding in the deal could be allocated toward starting up the production line, not just purchasing the actual missiles.

“The Air Force has been really tight-lipped about the details at like the unit cost level and the planned buy inventory for this program, starting with last year when it first moved it into the procurement side of the budget. So, it’s really hard to put an estimate on there, and there’s very few, like, comparable systems to compare it to, to try and get a rough cost estimate,” he said.

Haelig said the Army’s Dark Eagle hypersonic weapon is “a completely different system with much different procurement patterns and support systems,” and is “probably much more expensive than the ARRW would be.”

Gunzinger also suggested that the ARRW would have a lower price tag than the ground-launched Dark Eagle.

According to Army budget documents, the unit cost of an all-up round and canister for the Dark Eagle system in fiscal 2026 was nearly $37 million. However, the unit cost is expected to go down in the coming years.

One of the advantages of air-launched hypersonic weapons is that developers don’t have to build them with rocket boosters large enough to get them from the ground or surface level to higher altitudes before their glide body separates, Gunzinger said.

“You’re already at altitude and at speed when you launch a hypersonic weapon from an aircraft. So, that reduces the size and cost of air-launched hypersonic weapons. I think that dynamic is pretty important,” he added.

It’s unclear exactly when the Air Force will field the ARRW.

“I think the intent is to field these weapons and other hypersonic weapons as quickly as possible to restore our ability to deter China and other adversaries, as well as to prepare for contingency operations in the Pacific,” Gunzinger said. “So, I would hazard a guess, not knowing when the [initial operational capability] might be for the ARRW, but I would hazard a guess it’ll be this decade. It won’t be pushed into the 2030s. And of course, that’s not just a matter of how quickly the Air Force can complete testing and so forth with live rounds, but also how quickly Lockheed Martin can produce these weapons to reach an IOC threshold. But I suspect it’s going to be in a couple years, not another five to 10.”

Haelig predicted that it will take “multiple years” to get them out to units at scale.

The Air Force will have to train air crews and maintainers and prepare to integrate the system with the platforms that will be carrying the weapon, he noted.

“Much of that can be done ahead of the actual production at scale of the munition, so that once the munitions start coming off of the production line and being delivered to operational units, those platforms are actually ready to use them and to actually field them. So, if those two tracks are going in parallel, you buy back a lot of time. But the big constraint still remains how quickly they’ll be able to produce that,” he said.

In a press release issued Tuesday, Lockheed Martin said it has already funded “efforts, materials, and equipment required to start ARRW’s production, underscoring the company’s commitment to delivering this critical capability to the U.S. Air Force at speed and scale.”

The company announced that it broke ground on an expansion effort for Building P-20 in Troy, Alabama, that will add 47,000 square feet of production space for the ARRW program.

“The expansion will triple the current facility’s production space and generate new American jobs over the next four years,” according to the press release, which noted that the workforce will build ARRW using advanced manufacturing, robotics and digital technologies.

The post Air Force launches next phase of hypersonic missile program with $694M contract award for ARRW appeared first on DefenseScoop.
